doc.title: Ralph LaLama interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 23, 2010

title: What makes a wrong note
summary: LaLama distinguishes wrong notes from tension notes, citing Thad Jones, Monk, Rollins, and his singer wife's ears.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: That’s okay. I like long answers. I don’t know if I can phrase this question correctly, but in improvisation, in jazz improvisation, to you, what constitutes a wrong note?

Well okay that’s a good question. It’s like beauty is in the eyes of the beholder, okay? I think there are wrong notes. A lot of people don’t. I do. I really do. Because you have a background, you have a chord, and then you could use all twelve notes but it’s how you organize them. You know what I mean? It’s the organization. Sometimes you might put a wrong note in a wrong part of the beat or something, and it sounds wrong. And I just get

this tension up my spine. You know what I mean? But, then technically you can play a wrong note, technically meaning theoretically it could be a wrong note but it sounds right. You know, because of the placement. You know Thad Jones was the master of it. Coltrane too. Sonny Rollins, all those masters, Joe Henderson. As far as theoretically, in other words we have a chord, we have a scale and we have the chord tone. So if you play outside of that, it could be considered wrong. But if you know how to phrase it exactly right and resolve it right that’s another thing. It’s in the resolution. You can resolve a wrong note and make it right see. And then sometimes I know when I hit a wrong note, you know like I say I feel it up my spine, and I usually hear it from my wife.
No. My wife is a great singer, Nicole Pasternak, she’s a great singer.

And she has great ears too. You know what I mean? But I’m just saying I’m joking but I’m not. I’m serious about what I’m saying. But she doesn’t actually holler at me, but I know she can tell when I hit it. But when you’re trying to improvise, sometimes you get hung up. So if you just play all your licks that are comfortable, all your stuff, then you’re not going to mess up. Then I don’t think you’re really improvising. You know what I mean? I mean like Monk. Monk. Speaking of Monk, [scats] it’s obviously — not a wrong note — but it sounds right. It sounds — there’s tension. Let’s put it this way: there’s tension notes, and there’s wrong notes. Ah that’s very good Ralph.
We’ll quote you on that. You’ll make our little snippets of good quotes.
But I noticed yesterday in listening to you —
Well no, every once in a while you would end a phrase with a note that made me go, like literally, like gee I wish I would have thought of that. But it sounded pretty cool.

Well that’s what I mean. That was tension. That wasn’t wrong, hopefully. You know what I mean? I mean that’s the way I would interpret it. I don’t know, I’ve been doing that a lot more lately. I’ve been trying to get a little bit more modern. I don’t know, I don’t like that term, but in other words I’m just experimenting. And hopefully if all these improvisers do, you know, you don’t want to be complacent. I don’t. That’s boring to me. So I started a very concrete — but that’s not the — consonant, I was more consonant when I first started playing. Well this was actually a lot of my upstate influence. You know what I mean? And as I got older and you know you start hearing more, and you hear other guys too, I get influenced by other people too. I’ll be honest about that. I’m definitely influenced by what things are around me at the moment and at different places and in different cultures. Because I’m lucky, I get to go around the world.
